caption: Retired from service with United in 1934, this is the only surviving example of the Boeing Model 80 series. The airplane was later privately owned, barnstorming and conducting joy rides in the Pacific Northwest. It was also used as a flying electric billboard for night advertising in Southern California. In 1941, it became a cargo aircraft in Alaska. After the war, it was stored and then discarded. It was recovered from an Anchorage dump in 1960 and eventually brought to Seattle. The Model 80A-1 restoration project served as a catalyst for establishment of the Pacific Northwest Aviation Historical Foundation, which later became The Museum of Flight.

It sure doesn't feel like almost 12 years ago, but in late 2014 I spent a wonderful couple of hours on the southside of Ted Stevens on a crisp autumn morning. While the shadows got shorter as the sun rose from behind the Chugach Mountains, I watched as the morning’s freight rush departed from 7R. Every one of these big freighters, bathed in the sun's golden morning light, getting airborne for the long flights down south. It was plane spotting at it’s finest.

[9:18AM] This 32-year-old cargo workhorse still looks glorious as she departs for Cologne, Germany operating UPS203. Incredible visibility this morning made possible by bitter cold and low humidity; for reference, the radio towers below the nose are about 13 miles (21 kilometers) from where I was standing.
